title: Signal for rescue
summary: Three of anything is a distress signal: three fires, three whistle blasts, three flashes.

blocks.p: Three of anything is a distress signal: three fires in a triangle, three whistle blasts, three flashes. Repeat at intervals.

Ground-to-air symbols, in an open area and as large as you can make them, at least 20 ft (6 m) long and 3½ ft (1 m) wide, in strong contrast with the ground: V means you need assistance, X means you need medical help.

blocks.cap: Use branches, rocks, bright fabric or trampled snow against a contrasting background, in an open area.

blocks.p: Flash sunlight at aircraft with a signal mirror, or with any shiny object such as a polished belt buckle. Aim through a V of two fingers held out toward the aircraft, and flash in threes. Don’t keep the beam on the cockpit for more than a few seconds: it can blind the pilot.

blocks.cap: Sight the aircraft through the V of your fingers and aim the reflected light through the V.

blocks.p: In a hostile situation, remember that any signal can also show your position to people you don’t want to find you.

sources.name: Be Ready Utah (State of Utah), Emergency Signaling
sources.used: A series of three is an international distress signal; mirror: form a V with two fingers as a sight, aim the reflected light through it at the target, flash in threes; three fires in a triangle signal distress; bright colored items or contrasting rocks, dirt or branches for ground signals; a whistle carries farther than a voice

sources.name: Iowa Hunter Safety Course (hunter-ed.com, Kalkomey, with the Iowa DNR), Signaling for Help
sources.used: The international emergency sign for distress is three of any signal: three whistle blasts, three mirror flashes, three fires evenly spaced; make an X as large as possible

sources.name: US Army FM 21-76, Survival Manual, chapter 19 (pp. 200-208)
sources.used: Three fires in a triangle is the international distress signal; ground-to-air symbols at least 1 meter wide and 6 meters long, in contrast with the ground, in an open area easily spotted from the air; no mirror: polish a belt buckle or similar; do not keep the beam on the cockpit for more than a few seconds, it may blind the pilot; signals to friends may alert the enemy to your location

sources.name: Ground-to-air emergency code, FM 21-76 Figure 19-6 as reproduced on aircav.com (Codes and Signals, ch. 19 p. 4); FAA AIM 6-2-6 Ground-Air Visual Code text (faraim.org copy)
sources.used: V: require assistance; X: require medical assistance (figure labels, read from a third-party copy because the FAA and Army figures are images); AIM: symbols at least 10 feet high, maximum contrast with the background, made of fabric, wood, stones or tramped snow
